html:
On 15 July 1099 the armies of the First Crusade stormed Jerusalem after a siege of about five weeks. It was the goal of the expedition that Pope Urban II had called in 1095.

Urban answered a plea for help from the Byzantine emperor Alexios I Komnenos against the Seljuk Turks, who had overrun Anatolia. Tens of thousands of knights and common people from France, Germany and Norman Italy marched east through Constantinople. They took Nicaea in 1097 and Antioch in 1098 after long, starving sieges. By then the Fatimids of Egypt had taken Jerusalem back from the Seljuks.

When the walls fell, the crusaders massacred much of the Muslim and Jewish population, and the killing was remembered for generations. Godfrey of Bouillon became the first ruler of the Kingdom of Jerusalem, one of four crusader states on the coast of the Levant. They rebuilt the Church of the Holy Sepulchre. The kingdom held Jerusalem until Saladin took it in 1187, and the last crusader city fell in 1291.
